title: Beyond Data Centers: Growing Out of the Middle-Tech Trap
text:
Beyond Data Centers: Growing Out of the Middle-Tech Trap

Photo by MOHD RASFAN/AFP via Getty Images

By: Jonathan DasonThroughout history, smaller states have often maintained independence by carefully managing great power relations, balancing various trade and economic arrangements and military partnerships in an effort to resist excessive dependence on either side.Malaysia now finds itself amid a technological competition between the United States and China, each building its own technological ecosystem and stack. This rivalry has entered a new chapter driven by competing advancements in artificial intelligence (AI). Meanwhile, the global AI boom has spawned a wave of mega-campus data center development across the country.For an aspiring middle power with an upper-middle-income economy like Malaysia, it is not economically efficient, nor is it technologically feasible, for the country to compete with both the United States and China across the AI value chain. Despite the cost of developing a frontier model such as DeepSeek’s V3 being reportedly less than USD $6 million, it is not an amount that can be easily footed by a developing country like Malaysia. Thus, it is sensible for Malaysia to play the neutral card as far as possible by identifying strategic segments where it can build domestic capabilities while selectively integrating foreign capital and technology from both powers.The Middle-Technology TrapLike many other developing countries, Malaysia’s economy has historically grown by relying on foreign direct investment (FDI) and technology transfers from multinational corporations (MNCs). While that model has been successful at developing the country’s industrial capacity and laying the foundations for its current position within the global semiconductor supply chain, this technology diffusion and leapfrog model is not adequate if the country is to achieve its goals of transforming into a high-income, innovation-driven economy as outlined in the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan (MD2030) and the National AI Action Plan 2026-2030.The middle-technology trap occurs when countries adopt foreign technology but fail to develop domestic innovation and intellectual property. As one Malaysian Technology CEO puts it: “(the country) optimized for the ‘how’ (process excellence) while outsourcing the ‘what’ (intellectual property and product design) to multinational corporations.” This leaves the local ecosystem dependent on foreign technology, as businesses prioritize immediate returns over the risky, long-term nature of innovation. The economy consequently remains confined to lower-value segments of the global value chain, where modest income potential, low productivity growth and a lack of globally marketable domestic technology compounds to slow Malaysia’s transition into a high-income nation.The advent of AI adds a new dimension to this structural dilemma. Malaysia can host the AI boom by importing chips, building data centers to house them, and deploying foundation models; reaping short-term productivity gains yet never owning a piece of the underlying technology.Turning “Made in Malaysia” into “Made by Malaysia”Technology-focused industrial policy is not new to Malaysia. In the 1990s, the government established the Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC Malaysia) to accelerate the country’s digital economy. While successful in attracting investment, it delivered mixed results, falling short of its innovative ambitions. Learning from that experience, the MD2030 and the National AI Action Plan introduce the concept of “Made by Malaysia,” placing locally developed AI products and services at the core of its national aspirations. This is supported by outcome-based accountability structures designed to strengthen policy execution and foster an innovative ecosystem through bodies like AI Malaysia Berhad, which drives national implementation and cultivates intellectual property, patient capital, and institutional agility.Malaysia has also set 2030 targets that extend beyond data centers: raising the AI-anchored digital economy’s contribution to 30% of the national GDP, reaching the top 25 in the IMD World Digital Competitiveness Ranking, and aiming be among the top 10 in Stanford’s AI Index. It aims to also re-skill 700,000 workers, create 500,000 job opportunities, provide financing to 5,000 local technology companies, and produce five locally domiciled digital unicorns.Based on its plans, it is clear that Malaysia does not seek to build the next Nvidia, Anthropic, or Moonshot AI. Rather, it plans to complement and build on its existing strengths along the AI value chain without directly replicating or competing with the great powers.An area that stands out is the semiconductor industry, where Malaysia is the 6th largest semiconductor exporter globally, accounting for 13% of global assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP) volume. This puts Malaysia in a favorable position within the ATP segment of the AI value chain. The goal is to use this industrial base to move into adjacent, higher-value segments such as integrated circuit (IC) design. One such company is SykeChip, which listed on Bursa Malaysia earlier this year. SykeChip’s locally developed MARS1000 edge AI processor solves the problem of AI application dependency on the internet by handling part of the data processing directly on the device, greatly reducing latency while protecting privacy. Other Malaysian firms, such as Oppstar and Vitrox, have also started developing technologies that will expand on Malaysia’s technical niche.This is where the dual meaning from the concept of “Made by Malaysia” comes in. Ostensibly, it refers to technology developed in Malaysia or by Malaysians. However, it also carries a second meaning: technological sovereignty. The national plan calls for domestic control over critical parts of the technology stack, including sensitive data, essential infrastructure and applications involved in national decision-making.Essentially, Made by Malaysia distinguishes itself from autarky in this sector by recognizing the need for foreign technology and inputs. It applies only to critical systems as a calculated move to hedge Malaysia’s against global geopolitical risks.The Challenge AheadIndustrial policies often look good in theory, but the real challenge is in the execution. AI may advance faster than the speed at which the government can reskill workers and regulate new developments. Furthermore, the government cannot reliably predict specific technological trajectories nor dictate market-driven innovations.Ultimately, time will tell if the strategies that Malaysia puts in place will allow it to escape the middle-technology trap by moving beyond constructing data centers and charting its own path towards a high-income and high-technology nation.

About the Author

Jonathan Dason is a sustainability ecosystem builder working at the intersection of corporate sustainability and technology. He has multi-sector work experience ranging from Corporate, and Non-profit, to Government and Start-ups. Prior to his role as the Head of Product Strategy at Sustenyx, he was the founding hire of the Sustainability Centre of Excellence, where he helped build the function from inception and supported its integration into the wider organization at the Malaysian National Stock Exchange.
